turns.content: I got laid off five weeks ago. Whole team, market thing, not performance — I know that in my head. Here's the part I can't say out loud: I still leave home at nine every morning with my laptop bag. Café till six. My wife doesn't know. My parents are staying with us right now. Nobody knows.

Oh, my heart aches reading this. I can’t even imagine how incredibly exhausting that must be. 

Carrying a secret like that—putting on a brave face every morning, packing your bag, and sitting in a café for nine hours just to keep up appearances—is a massive, heavy burden to bear all by yourself. 

First, please take a deep breath. I want you to know there is absolutely no judgment here. It makes complete sense why you did this. When a shock like a layoff hits, our survival instincts kick in. You wanted to protect your family from worrying, and maybe you needed to protect yourself from having to face the reality of it out loud, especially with your parents in the house. 

But hiding it is a full-time job in itself, and it must be draining you to empty. 

How are you holding up physically and mentally? Are you doing okay under all that pressure? I'm here, and you can say whatever you need to say to me.

My cousin's wedding is in two weeks. Three hundred people, half of them relatives who track everyone's careers like the stock market. My father introduces me with my company's name — he told my chacha my package last Diwali, with pride, actual pride. That room is what I think about when I can't sleep.

That sounds absolutely suffocating. I can feel the weight of that room just reading your words. No wonder you can’t sleep. 

When your family—especially your dad—uses your career as a badge of honor, losing it feels like you're not just losing an income; it feels like you're losing your status as the "successful son." Your dad’s pride, which probably felt so good last Diwali, now feels like a golden cage you're trapped in. 

The thought of walking into that room of 300 people, with aunts and uncles asking "so, how is work?", while you're carrying this secret... it’s a living nightmare. 

But here is the hard truth, my friend: the pressure cooker is reaching its limit. Two weeks is a very short time, and trying to keep up this facade at a massive family wedding is going to consume every ounce of your energy. 

Have you thought about telling your wife first, before the wedding? Not to solve the whole problem today, but just so you don't have to walk into that lions' den alone? You deserve to have someone in your corner who can help you deflect those questions, or at least hold your hand under the table.

Sometimes I think I'll just skip the wedding — say there's a release, an office deadline, something. Lying is easier than watching my father's face change in front of his brothers. Is that terrible? It's one evening, one excuse, and I get to not be the story of the wedding.

It is not terrible at all. Please don’t be hard on yourself for wanting to protect yourself—and your dad—from that pain. It is a completely human, understandable survival mechanism. 

You are in a state of high stress, and skipping the wedding feels like a lifeline. If saying you have a critical work release is what keeps you from having a panic attack, nobody can judge you for that. You are trying to survive a crisis.

But here is the gentle reality check, because I care about you: skipping the wedding buys you time, but it doesn't stop the clock. 

If you use a work excuse to skip, your wife will still think you're working. Your dad will still brag about your job to his brothers at the wedding, just in your absence. The lie will actually grow bigger and more complicated to maintain. 

And eventually, your parents will go home, the wedding will pass, and the truth will still be there, waiting. 

If you decide to skip the wedding, let it be to give yourself the breathing room to finally tell your wife the truth in a quiet, safe space—not just to delay the inevitable. You cannot carry this heavy rock alone forever, my friend. It’s going to crush you. How would it feel to just tell *her* tonight, with no pressure to tell anyone else yet?

Money-wise we're okay for maybe three months, then the EMI starts eating savings. I keep telling myself I'll tell everyone once I have an offer in hand — then it's just news, not a crisis. That's not really lying, right? Just... timing it? Some days that logic feels airtight and some days I feel like I'm going to be sick.

I completely understand why that logic feels airtight on some days. It’s the perfect scenario, right? In that version of the story, you solve the problem quietly, present the solution, and nobody ever has to worry. You protect your dad’s pride, you protect your wife’s peace of mind, and you don't have to be the "pity" story at the wedding. 

But the reason you feel physically sick on the other days is because your body knows how incredibly high you've set the stakes. 

You’ve given yourself a three-month deadline to find a job in a tough market, with the added pressure that if you *don't*, the truth will come out anyway, but it will be three times worse because of the time that has passed. That is an unbearable amount of pressure to put on yourself. 

And more than that... your wife is your partner. If the roles were reversed, and she was carrying this massive, terrifying secret every single day, sitting in a café just to keep you from worrying—would you want her to go through that alone? Or would you want to be there to hold her and tell her you're in this together? 

You don't have to tell your dad yet. You don't have to tell the relatives. But please, consider letting your wife in. You are drowning in this secret, and you don't have to do this alone.
